title: Spotify's shuffle wasn't broken. Randomness was.
subtitle: Why a provably fair algorithm felt rigged — and why the fix was to make it less random

vo.text: In twenty fourteen, Spotify users were furious. The shuffle, they said, was broken.
It wasn't broken. But they weren't wrong either.
It keeps playing the same artist. Fix your shuffle. I pay for this. Thousands of them, saying the same thing.
So Spotify checked. The shuffle was Fisher-Yates. Every possible ordering exactly equally likely.
Provably uniform. There was no bug.
Here is one perfectly fair shuffle. Ten artists, ten songs each. This is what fair actually looks like.
Nine back-to-back repeats in a hundred songs, from the correct algorithm. The users were reporting it accurately.
So which of these is random? Almost everyone picks the even one. The even one is the fake.
Londoners were certain the flying bombs were aimed. The clusters were obvious. Whole districts, they said, were being targeted.
An actuary counted them. Five hundred and thirty-seven bombs, five hundred and seventy-six squares.
Zero point nine three per square. The same number, twice. A cluster is not a plan. It is what randomness looks like.
So Spotify stopped being fair. Group by artist, space them evenly, offset at random, then add a little jitter.
Less random by every measure that exists. Far more random to a human being. Engineers call it blue noise.
When the maths is right and it still feels wrong, the feeling is data too.
